The V6 engine model now incorporates sub-harmonics like 0.5 * f0 (3-cylinder bank order) and 0.333 * f0 (crankshaft 1st order) to achieve a deep, resonant sound. Analysis reveals that these sub-harmonics are essential, as relying solely on f0 leads to a thin sound.

Further realism will be added by introducing cycle-to-cycle combustion jitter, modeled as filtered stochastic frequency modulation (FM) and amplitude modulation (AM) to simulate the variability of real combustion. The jitter will modulate the frequency (0.25% FM jitter) and amplitude (6% AM jitter) within specific bands (30–250 Hz), breaking the sterile quality of a perfectly repeating digital model.


Analysis now incorporates overrun effects during braking (`throttle < 0.15`) using cylinder deactivation and wastegate bypass to increase exhaust roughness. A harmonic series is being constructed based on crankshaft phase, incorporating harmonics of crank rotation. The fundamental V6 firing frequency ($f_0$) and its harmonics, including half-order sub-harmonics, are used.


Exhaust simulation integrates asymmetric tube/exhaust saturation and modulated combustion air-pulse noise for realistic chuffing sounds. A Multi-Formant Exhaust Resonator Bank uses bandpass and shelf filters to simulate the formants of the exhaust, airbox, and tailpipe, resonating at specific frequencies with gentle Q. This model naturally blooms harmonics as RPM changes. The goal is to make the sound accurate to the physics.
